item.title: Big Earth Hackathon: Wildland Fire Challenge
item.description: Stanford Events — Big Earth Hackathon: Wildland Fire Challenge bridges the gap between innovation and impact by bringing Stanford students together with real-world stakeholders to design, build, and prototype solutions to one of today’s most pressing global systems crises — wildfire. Big Earth Hackathon is a 9 week challenge and optional companion course launching fall quarter at Stanford, open to undergraduates, graduate students, and postdocs across all disciplines at Stanford. Teams will tackle some of the most pressing wildfire challenges – from early detection and suppression, to fuel management, to community prevention – developing technology solutions using a user-centered design approach. Teams hear directly from practitioners and stakeholders who define the needs, and are supported by technical workshops throughout the quarter. Location: Y2E2 Building

item.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
item.description: Stanford Events — The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future. The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist. item.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
item.description: Stanford Events — Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition. Location: Green Library, Bing Wing

item.title: Suicide Assessment and Treatment: An Update for Professionals
item.description: Stanford Events — Overview8:30 AM (PST) - 2:00 PM (PST) | 11:30 AM (EST) - 5:00 PM (EST) With suicide rates increasing by 30% in the last 2 decades, suicide remains a pressing public health challenge. This course provides an overview of key topics in suicide assessment, prevention, and treatment that is relevant to all treatment settings and clinical disciplines. This course will cover assessment factors such as family history, past trauma, social isolation, and support systems and cultural/religious beliefs that stigmatize mental health or suicide. Prevention topics addressed will cover recognizing warning signs, responding to crises, and connecting individuals to appropriate resources and enhancing social support networks and community resilience. Putting concepts into practice, the course will also cover treatment methods such as psychotherapy, medication, hospitalization for acute risk or severe mental health crises, collaborative care models, follow-up care and ongoing monitoring. item.title: E-IPER Dissertation Defense: Anaïs Voşki
item.description: Stanford Events — Please join us for an E-IPER dissertation defense by Anaïs Voşki: "From the ocean floor to outer space: Awe and the overview effect as pathways to pro-environmental psychological and behavioral change." In-person: Y2E2 299 Virtual: Zoom webinar (passcode: 602030) ABSTRACT International consensus affirms that addressing the global environmental crisis requires transformative shifts in values and practices that center the fundamental interconnectedness between humans and nature, yet scalable psychological pathways toward such shifts remain elusive. Self-transcendent experiences—mental states characterized by reduced self-focus and increased connectedness beyond the self, such as awe, psychedelic, and peak experiences—offer one potential pathway. The overview effect, defined as the profound psychological shift reported by astronauts when viewing Earth from space, offers an exemplary case with both transformative potential and a distinctive pro-environmental profile. item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
item.description: Stanford Events — Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet. Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm. Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening. Location: McMurtry Building

item.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Gregor Steinbrügge- "Coupled Thermal-Orbital Evolution of the Galilean Satellites"
item.description: Stanford Events — Io's volcanism and Europa's surface bear witness to the dynamics driven by tidal interactions of the Galilean moons with Jupiter. While Europa and Ganymede host subsurface oceans, which makes them prime candidates for habitability, tidal heating is unlikely to have been constant over the age of the Laplace resonance. In this talk I will revisit the coupled thermal–orbital evolution of the Galilean satellites using the astrometric and geophysical constraints obtained over the past years. The Juno mission has provided additional data about geodetic parameters and recent ground-based observations indicate that Io has been volcanically active for most of its history, with potentially higher activity at earlier times. We also apply lessons learned from the Saturn system, particularly informed by the Cassini mission, to investigate the possibility of ‘resonance locking’ as the dominant mechanism driving the orbital migration of Io. item.title: Leonid Gozman — After Putin, After the War: Russia’s Next Chapter
item.description: Stanford Events — Neither Vladimir Putin nor the war in Ukraine will last forever. What political order is likely to follow, and what would it mean for Russia, Ukraine, and the West? Leonid Gozman, a longtime Russian opposition politician and political psychologist, will examine the scenarios that may unfold. A Ukrainian defeat, he argues, would likely produce a new war almost immediately. The end of Putin’s rule poses its own risks, and the transition could prove more dangerous than the present. Yet Gozman contends that a post-Putin Russia would probably be better for its citizens and the international community, even if members of Putin’s circle remain in power. That transition, he suggests, may open a narrow window for Russia to resume a path of normal political and economic development. This discussion will consider what such a path would require, what forces could close it, and what role domestic actors and Western governments might play in shaping the outcome. item.description: Stanford Events — The Creative Writing Program is pleased to announce the next event in the Lane Lecture Series: A Reading with Martín Espada. This event is open to Stanford affiliates and the general public. Registration is encouraged but not required. Register here ____ Martín Espada has published more than twenty books as a poet, editor, essayist, and translator. His latest book of poems is called Jailbreak of Sparrows (2025). His previous book, Floaters, won the National Book Award for Poetry in 2021. He is the editor of What Saves Us: Poems of Empathy and Outrage in the Age of Trump (2019). Espada has received the Ruth Lilly Poetry Prize, the Shelley Memorial Award, the PEN/Revson Fellowship, a Letras Boricuas Fellowship, and a Guggenheim Fellowship. item.title: Alain Schläpfer — Why Do Voters Elect Authoritarians? How Scandal Signals Independence from Elites
item.description: Stanford Events — Politicians who openly display anti-democratic traits can attract substantial electoral support, even among voters who value democracy. This paper argues that the very behavior that makes a politician objectionable can also reassure voters that the politician will remain independent of political elites. Voters whose preferred policies lie far from elite interests worry that the candidates they elect will be captured by elites once in office. Because capturing a politician mired in scandal is costly for elites, scandalous behavior can credibly signal that a candidate is beyond elite reach. Where elites are democratically committed, displays of anti-democratic intent become an efficient way to generate such a scandal. Voters may elect these candidates even though they are more likely to manipulate elections once in office, an outcome costly for voters and elites alike. item.title: Stanford Energy Seminar | Soft Materials for Hard Sustainability Challenges: Water production, Data center Sustainability, and High-Temperature Heat | Carlos Diaz-Marin, Stanford University
item.description: Stanford Events — The Stanford Energy Seminar has been a mainstay of energy engagement at Stanford for nearly 20 years and is one of the flagship programs of the Precourt Institute for Energy. We aim to bring a wide variety of perspectives to the Stanford community – academics, entrepreneurs, utilities, non-profits, and more. About the talk Water scarcity, rising energy demand, and global emissions are major sustainability challenges of the 21st century. This talk will highlight three soft matter-enabled technologies that the Diaz-Marin lab is developing to tackle these challenges. First, he will present their multiscale design of hydrogel-salt composites to produce water from air in any geography and at costs comparable to those of tap water. Secondly, he will show how low temperature carbon capture sorbents could transform AI into carbon-negative and water-positive by enabling data center heat reuse for carbon removal. item.title: Ivetta Sergeeva — The Authoritarian Passport: How States Discipline Emigrants
item.description: Stanford Events — Citizenship is conventionally understood as a source of rights and protection. It is also a source of dependency: states retain distinctive authority over passports, legal identities, civil status, and mobility that citizens need even when they live abroad. Under authoritarianism, these dependencies become instruments of political control. The study introduces extraterritorial authoritarian citizenship, a continuing relationship in which emigrants depend on origin-state institutions whose provision of nominally universal rights is politically conditional. It generates latent leverage: the capacity to impose costs without exercising it against anyone in particular. Emigrants may curb dissent even when never targeted, and transnational repression activates leverage already at work. item.title: Film Screening of the Latvian submission for the Academy Awards – Ulya
item.description: Stanford Events — Join us for a film screening of Latvia's submission for the Academy Awards and commentary from Dr. Karla Oeler, Director of the Center for Russian, Eastern European, and Eurasian Studies and Associate Professor of Film and Media Studies in the Department of Art & Art History. Ulya (2026) is a true story about Uljana Semjonova, who is a very tall girl living on a remote farm in Soviet Latvia in 1964. Her height, almost two meters, worries her family, who aren't sure how she will fit into the world. When her class photo reaches basketball coaches, she is taken to Riga to train with TTT Riga. She works hard but feels torn, because basketball doesn't give her the ordinary life she dreams of. After running away back home, she realizes that both the village and the sport see her only as "the tall girl."
